content:
Apple has been given until Monday to respond to a complaint filed by Epic Games with the Brazilian antitrust regulator, in which Epic accuses Apple of interpreting restrictively its various obligations under the recent App Store antitrust agreement reached in Brazil. Details below.

A little bit of background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it would now allow developers to distribute apps in Brazil through alternative app marketplaces.

This change was part of a settlement to resolve a years-long antitrust investigation prompted by a complaint from Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods other than Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. You can read more about the structure here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to Brazilian newspaper O Globo (via MacMagazine) today, Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of setting up "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical feasibility of alternative app distribution.

Epic says that, although the new terms in Brazil apply only to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "explicitly covers iPadOS."

The company also reportedly objects to what it calls "scare screens" designed to deter users from installing apps from outside the App Store; it is also unhappy with the current installation flow, which it says requires nine steps, compared with six for Apple's current implementation in Europe.

Epic added, per O Globo, that Apple's original installation flow in Europe required 15 steps, and after being ordered to reduce it to six, "the download abandonment rate dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is needed to calculate fees" and argued that this allows the company to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
